## Topics

### Systems Biology and Cancer Niche Theory
The emerging framework that cancer arises from the breakdown of healthy tissue niches into cancer-permissive niches, shifting focus from killing cancer cells to restoring the tissue microenvironment. Key contributors include Mena Bissell, Carlos Sonenshein, and Anne Soto.
*_(~30% of transcript; Sections 2-17)_*

### Extended Evolutionary Synthesis (EES)
The set of extensions to the modern synthesis that emphasizes developmental processes occurring within an organism's lifetime and argues that cancer dysfunction cannot be reduced to genetic mutations alone.
*_(~10% of transcript; Sections 8-9)_*

### Autonomic Nervous System and Stress Signaling in Tumor Progression
Recent findings on how the peripheral autonomic nervous system and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal neuroendocrine signaling influence tumor growth, metastasis, and arterial blood flow to cancer sites.
*_(~15% of transcript; Sections 21-23)_*

### Allostatic Load and Chronic Stress as Cancer Risk Factors
The concept of allostasis and cumulative allostatic load as a mechanism linking chronic stress and behavioral factors to cancer-promoting physiological changes, including steroid receptor activation and immune dysregulation.
*_(~10% of transcript; Sections 24-25)_*

### Bowen Theory Parallels to Systems Biology
Recurring comparisons between Bowen family systems theory concepts—chronic anxiety, differentiation of self, multigenerational transmission, and identified patient—and systems biology principles such as emergence, niche regulation, and relational biology.
*_(~15% of transcript; Sections 10-11, 19-21)_*

### Patient Agency and Adaptation to Cancer Diagnosis
Discussion of how a patient's confidence in their treatment decisions, sense of control, and ability to adapt to a cancer diagnosis correlate with outcomes, illustrated by a cancer registry interview study and clinical observations.
*_(~10% of transcript; Sections 28-30)_*

### Conrad Waddington and Foundational Systems Biology Concepts
Waddington's contributions to systems biology, epigenetics, and evolutionary developmental biology, including his central question about how networks of cellular interaction produce organized organs with unitary character.
*_(~5% of transcript; Section 4)_*
